title: Gloria Steinem, pioneering feminist activist and journalist, dies at 92
dek: Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist activist and journalist who co-founded Ms. magazine and the National Women's Political Caucus, died at her home in New York City on September 2, 2026, at age 92. No cause of death was disclosed.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Gloria Steinem died at age 92 at her home in New York City on September 2, 2026, surrounded by loved ones.
bottom_line: Steinem's death marks the end of an era of direct leadership from the second-wave feminist movement. The immediate question is whether the organizations she built and the causes she championed will sustain momentum as the movement confronts renewed threats to reproductive rights and ongoing gaps in workplace and political representation.
body:
Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist activist and journalist who gave voice to second-wave feminism and transformed how American women understood their place in society, died at her home in New York City on September 2, 2026, at age 92. She was surrounded by loved ones. No cause of death was given.
Steinem was born March 25, 1934, in Toledo, Ohio. She did not attend school regularly until age 11, after her parents divorced. In 1956, Steinem graduated from Smith College with a degree in government. She spent two years in India on a fellowship after college, pursuing journalism in New York upon her return.
In 1963, Steinem went undercover as a Playboy bunny and wrote an exposé for Show magazine titled "A Bunny's Tale" about poor working conditions. The article brought her early visibility as a journalist investigating women's labor.
In 1968, Steinem became a founding editor and political columnist for New York magazine. In 1969, Steinem published an article titled "After Black Power, Women's Liberation" that cemented her place as a feminist icon. In 1971, months before establishing her signature publication, Steinem helped form the National Women's Political Caucus. In 1971, she co-founded Ms. magazine, which started as an insert in New York magazine before becoming its own standalone publication in 1972. In 1976, Ms. magazine became the first national publication to spotlight domestic violence on its cover.
Steinem co-founded the Ms. Foundation for Women, the Free to Be Foundation, and the Women's Media Center. She also helped establish Equality Now, Donor Direct Action, and Direct Impact Africa as international links. She married businessman and animal rights activist David Bale in September 2000. Bale died three years later from primary brain lymphoma.
The gains from her activism are measurable. When the National Women's Political Caucus began, there were 15 women elected to Congress; today there are 150. When it began, there were 363 women state legislators; today there are 2,476. When it began, there were only seven women city mayors; today there are 428, according to NPR.
Steinem earned the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's top civilian honor, which she received in 2013 from President Barack Obama. Obama said at the time: "Because of her work, across America and around the world, more women are afforded the respect and opportunities that they deserve. She also changed how women thought about themselves." In 2019, Steinem received the Freedom Award from the National Civil Rights Museum. In 2020, a feature film titled "The Glorias, A Life on The Road" was made based on her 2015 memoir and starred Julianne Moore. At age 91, Steinem collaborated on a picture book with Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee titled "Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All," published in February 2026.
In 2022, a few weeks before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, Steinem told NPR that she did not think the work on reproductive justice would be in vain. When Steinem returned from India to begin her journalism career, she was briefly involved with a CIA-backed organization that sent American students to Soviet-sponsored youth festivals. She later defended her role in that arrangement.
